title: Dave in Love Part One
summary: After an opening conversation about a private participant trying to conceive, David Choe, Asa Akira, Valentin, Money Mark and Steve Lee introduce the show. Asa reports her book entering a second printing and describes audiobook work; David returns from Hawaii and uses airport inconvenience, wealth and a confused argument about millennials to examine his habit of escaping difficulty. He says a major television project collapsed because the network found him too extreme, leaving him time for an intensive Hawaii therapy retreat. The podcast calls itself therapy, but the cast also calls it the Enablers Club and acknowledges that it replaced licensed treatment while encouraging dangerous ideas. David invites his aging parents, Critter, Harry Kim, a Mexico City partner, a former lover and another recurring woman in succession, then admits that every visit prevented the solitude he claimed to seek. A debate about whether pornography and DVDASA help anyone is unusually self-critical: entertainment and listener connection are weighed against damaged relationships, employment consequences, family strain and the podcast's cost to Asa. David connects service, creative maturation and thinking about another person to a hoped-for exit from arrested development. The title story begins when a private woman messages him after seeing him at a Kona restaurant. They talk for hours and rapidly build an intense relationship before meeting. Her prior-partner stories, private social media and apparent alignment with David's checklist make her seem both ideal and suspicious. A misunderstanding turns 'baby sister' and 'two mortgages' into an imagined child; David uses stigmatizing disability and body language while calling his willingness to raise that nonexistent child a breakthrough. When she panics and asks for time, he insists on an immediate public meeting, waits for eight hours, threatens to remain until he starves or dies, returns after being told the parking lot is closed and sends a confrontation video. Her brother reports a panic attack. The editorial record treats those actions as coercive pressure, not romance. David and the cast then speculate about catfishing, sex, gender and sociopathy, while his therapist reportedly reframes the attachment as evidence he can feel again. David declares the unseen woman his girlfriend and says he is in love; Part One ends without proving her identity, mutual relationship status or whether they ever meet. Every idea and offensive term remains as source evidence, while the private woman's name, business, family, phone, accounts, exact locations and health trail remain undiscoverable. Ten empty zero-duration records are the only cleaner drops, and no line receives a published speaker name.
source_notes: All ten cleaner removals are empty zero-duration records; raw and clean word counts are identical.
The automated review queue is empty. Canonical name/title repairs are accepted, but health podcast remains literal rather than becoming invented prose.

The opening explicitly names David Choe, Asa Akira, Valentin, Money Mark and Steve Lee. Presence truth does not create turn truth because the artifact has zero diarized turns and zero identity windows.
The private woman is not identified. Her salon, family, phone, accounts, exact Kona/Los Angeles locations, charity mentions and father health trail cannot be combined into an identity dossier.
The central child story is a misunderstanding: baby sister was heard as babysitter, and two mortgages was heard as taking care of two people. No child exists in the account.
David's disability, body, racial, transgender and addiction language remains source evidence. Slurs and unsupported diagnoses are never promoted into editorial labels.

The woman's panic, refusal to meet and request for time remain authoritative. Waiting, threatened self-harm, returning after closure and sending a confrontation video are pressure tactics, not evidence of romance or consent.
David calls her his girlfriend and says he is in love. Part One does not independently establish mutual status, identity, catfishing, sex/gender, or an eventual meeting.
The unnamed network series and unaired episodes remain described at the level David supplies; no network or unreleased footage is inferred.
The podcast's own benefit claims are balanced by its explicit accounts of employment, romantic, family and financial costs.
speaker_policy: Episode-level metadata may record the five explicitly introduced public participants. Because diarization yielded zero turns and zero identity windows, no dialogue is assigned to David Choe, Asa Akira, Valentin, Money Mark, Steve Lee, Scrotum Coat, Alex or anyone else.

connections.why: Sexual-position and gravity talk is entertainment, not evidence-based fertility guidance.
The cast's uncertainty about the definition exposes how a label becomes a moral shortcut.
Money lets David leave difficult projects, recreating the avoidance he attributes to youth.
Gambling abstinence is followed by deliberate workaholism rather than a neutral end to compulsion.
Institutional financing offers reach but conflicts with the conduct a network expected from a host.
Disclosure and friendship can help while an enabling entertainment room remains distinct from licensed treatment.
An aging parent's limits turn abstract wealth into a finite scheduling decision.
Every meaningful visitor is defensible alone, but together they erase the retreat's stated purpose.
The speakers test whether truth is always kinder than a face-saving lie.
Delegating the phone and then breaking a self-imposed check schedule mirrors other addiction loops.
Asa frames sexual performance as modest utility without claiming universal social importance.
Employment, family and relationship losses are first-person evidence against measuring value only by audience enjoyment.
MCA becomes a model for growing beyond an early transgressive identity without erasing it.
Responsibility for another person is described as both marriage's burden and its benefit.
A public figure turns being spotted into direct private contact, collapsing audience and intimacy.
Two misheard phrases support an elaborate child story before basic facts are checked.
Desired traits are explicitly built from prior injuries and exclusions rather than this person's known reality.
Intense mutual attraction does not cancel a request for time or refusal to meet.
Threatening to starve or die transfers responsibility and pressure to the other person.
Voice, photos and search matches do not prove who the private person is.
One participant's declaration of love and relationship cannot establish the unseen person's agreement.
A healthier relationship is joked about as a threat to self-destruction content and a new worker's job.

content_warnings: ableist slurs about an imagined child
